newsitem.title: USA: MCI says considers merger with British Telecom.
newsitem.headline: MCI says considers merger with British Telecom.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp., in what would be one of the biggest corporate mergers ever, said Friday it was in talks to be acquired by British Telecommunications Plc.
British Telecom already holds a 20 percent stake in MCI, the nation's second-largest long distance provider.

Washington-based MCI said it expected the talks to be concluded this weekend, although it noted that there were no guarantees an agreement would be reached. "MCI anticipates that its deliberations will be concluded this weekend and an announcement will be made prior to Monday morning," it said.

Industry analysts speculated that a final deal would price MCI at about $40 per share, making the 80 percent that British Telecom does not own worth $22.1 billion, based on MCI's 691 million shares outstanding.

They applauded the talks, saying a combination of the two companies would be a good fit in the super-competitive U.S. long distance phone industry, where MCI and No. 3 Sprint have been battling an ailing AT&T Corp.

"This is an extremely competitive business, and horizontal mergers like this make sense," said Allen Sinai, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Global Economic Advisors. "The economies of scale in this case could be considerable, and the leverage in terms of potential profits is high ... It would be good purchase."
A spokesman for British Telecom confirmed the British company was interested in a merger with MCI.

British Telecom is aiming to offer a mixture of cash and stock for the 80 percent of MCI it does not own, a source close to the deal told Reuters. The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said a price was still not finalised, but said an announcment was expected on Sunday, if not before.
"It would be a good fit for British Telecom and provide a major foothold in this country," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
"It wouldn't take away from the long-distance battle. Before that's over, there will be losers and winners," he added.

In Washington, lawyers and analysts said a deal would likely win approval of U.S. regulators. "It appears this deal would pass (Federal Communications Commission) approval at first glance," said Scott Cleland of the Washington Research Group of Schawb Capital Markets.

An FCC rule adopted last year permits a foreign carrier to invest in a U.S. carrier in excess of a 25 percent cap, as long as the overseas company's home market is open for competition from U.S. telecommunications companies.
Under the rule, adopted last November, an investment stake of more than 25 percent by a foreign phone company triggers an automatic FCC review of that company's home market.

Scott Harris, a former head of the FCC's international bureau and now an attorney with Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, said that other than the U.S. telecommunications market, the British market is the "most open" in the world.

MCI's stock was halted for trading at $27.25, up $1.875 on Nasdaq, although it jumped as much as $5 to $30.625 after CNBC television reported that the companies were talking. The exchange said it would investigate those trades.
Shares of British Telecom traded in New York were down $2.125 at $55.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
